extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians and comedy writers (beginners/intermediates)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for writing and performing stand-up comedy, covering comedic styles, setup/punchline mechanics, tags, and the underlying concept of comedic conflict (safety + violation). Intended to help writers craft jokes that land on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-Liners (style)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-Liner comedians use quick, snappy lines that have all the information you need to get the joke. They bounce around from topic to topic with little or no segue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengths: require no long setups, easy to try out on stage, not likely to leave you stuck if a joke bombs. Weaknesses: often sound unnatural for new comedians and many comedians 'graduate' to storytelling; better at premises than extended expansion. Use as a starting place; if a one-liner bombs you can switch back to a proven joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling (style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Storytellers take a single premise and make it into an entire, logical story that can build massive momentum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengths: allows expansion and audience identification with characters/POV; feels natural. Weaknesses: harder to perform initially; if the story bombs you can get stuck and have trouble segueing. Stories often start from a single joke that snowballs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational vs. Experience-Based Continuum
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational humor is third-person, about seeing the world in a new light; experience-based humor is first-person, coming from your life (e.g., Ray Romano).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most comedians sit between the extremes and can mix both in a set. Observational suits people good at reframing common situations; experience-based suits those mining personal stories. Experiment with both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Current Event Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor dealing with what’s going on in the world right now; useful to lead off a show and make your material feel 'in the moment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: signals freshness and spontaneity to the audience. Downsides: often low quality because you can't test it and it has a short shelf-life (gets dated quickly). Use sparingly and as openers, but be aware of testing constraints and rapid obsolescence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes tailored to the specific place or audience; brings the show 'into the moment' and signals you are speaking to this audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: great opener to gain trust and feel local. Downsides: limited testing opportunities and double-risk if used as an opener (can backfire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal Humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Material that 'works anywhere' — understandable regardless of region; deals with what makes people the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary for touring nationally/internationally. Expect to spend most of your time here if you plan to tour. Universal humor contrasts with local humor and should be prioritized for broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not have to choose only one comedy style; you are allowed to jump between styles within the same performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for beginners: play around with one-liners, current events, and stories to find what 'chooses you.' Variety makes sets more interesting and aids learning which style fits you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup Definition and Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A setup is the factual part of a line that leads up to the joke. It is clear and concise and must be easily identifiable to the majority of the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setups introduce the topic, get the audience on the same page, and contain all the information (words, gestures, voice, context, expressions, POV, opinions, mood) an audience member needs to get the joke. If the setup is weak, the punchline will fall flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups: Clarity and Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Setups should be extremely easy to understand (clear and concise) and should not have TOO MUCH information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overloading setup with unnecessary details. Keep the essential facts that the audience needs to build a prediction; extra information can slow the click-point and dilute the payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups: Use Non-Verbal Communication and POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Only ~7% of communication is verbal; setups should leverage tone, body language, gestures, and convey your POV/opinion/emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-verbal elements often convey emotions and make setups more effective. Convey your point-of-view so the setup does more than just describe a situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups: Be Interesting and Conversational
rubrics_metrics.description: Great setups are interesting in themselves and sound natural/conversational rather than 'I’m writing a setup.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize every moment on stage — don't treat setups as space-fillers. Avoid the 'comedy mindset' filter while writing (which leads to hacky, generic setups and writer's block). Write naturally and let setups be engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups Should Not Be the Goal
rubrics_metrics.description: If you tell yourself 'I’m writing a setup for a punchline' you’ll adopt an unnatural mindset and produce hacky material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing setups; focus on natural conversation and authentic points-of-view. Perfect setups make punchlines come more quickly, but don't obsess over crafting a setup in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup as Foundation for Punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The main job of the setup is to introduce the topic and create an intriguing story; it enables the punchline to operate as a payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer setups are acceptable when introducing new bits to give the audience time to 'shift gears.' Ensure setups provide the necessary context for the punchline's reckoning/resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline Principle: Let the Audience Decide
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience (and the audience alone) decides if something is funny; writers should give jokes several stage tries before cutting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance/testing matters; sometimes material fails for performance/context reasons. Use staged feedback to judge keeping or cutting material — writing is only an initial guess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchlines: Keep Audience Demographics in Mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing punchlines, consider age, sex, social status, political views, etc.; different markets favor different types of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clean comedy works in every market; blue humor works primarily in bars/nightclubs. Tailor material to the audience you want to speak to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline Structure: Playful Surprise and Keywords
rubrics_metrics.description: A punchline is the payoff that contains the surprise; along with the surprise it usually contains a keyword or phrase that defines the meaning of the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keywords typically occur toward the end of the sentence and often 'define' the punchline (not necessarily change the meaning). The surprise must also 'please' (be playful), not just be unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyword Placement and Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep keywords at the end of the punchline to avoid 'stepping on the laughs' and to allow the click-point to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience is laughing you don't need to add more info. Wrong placement (e.g., placing the keyword earlier and trailing more words) can reduce impact. Aim for the click-point shortly after the keyword (shorter click-points increase laugh size).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyword Phonetics (Hard Consonant Theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keywords often end in hard consonants (e.g., B, D, K, P, T, M, N) and these are commonly thought to be funnier than words ending in soft vowel sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a general rule and not absolute — don't reword a joke solely to get a hard consonant ending if it harms the joke elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Click-Point: Fast Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A click-point is the time it takes the audience to go from keyword to understanding; faster click-points produce bigger laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a short click-point (the guide suggests ~0.3 seconds after the keyword if everything lines up). Reduce processing time by tightening wording and removing distractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline Length: Short and Sweet
rubrics_metrics.description: Punchlines should be concise (like a whip) to retain the 'snap' that produces comedic energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a punchline is too long, shorten by: splitting into multiple sentences, deleting supporting but unnecessary words, or using contractions/abbreviations. A punchline can never be too short provided all necessary info remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline Drafting: Iterate and Search
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't stop at the first few punchline ideas; keep searching because the first punchline found is often the most logical and least funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are dozens of possible punchlines for any setup. Trying more options cannot hurt; you can always revert to an earlier version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taglines: Punchline-on-Punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: A tagline is a punchline on top of a punchline — using the previous punchline as the setup for another payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taglines increase laughs-per-minute by getting more jokes from the same setup. They are not substitutes for the original punchline; they rely on that punchline as setup. Use tags instead of starting a new joke when the audience is still laughing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke Processing Steps (Constructing, Reckoning, Resolving)
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences 'get a joke' through three ordered steps: 1) Constructing — building an understanding of the setup; 2) Reckoning — recognizing an inconsistency or problem (often triggered by the keyword); 3) Resolving — changing the representation to make sense of the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write setups to make the 'constructing' easy (help audience pick important info), craft keywords that create a strong reckoning shift, and deliver a resolution that reinterprets the setup cleanly so the audience can say 'Oh! I get the joke.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Keywords as Make-or-Break Moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Keywords are the words that cause the shift (reckoning); without the correct keyword the joke can stop being a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose keywords that produce a clear before-and-after mental switch. If replacing a keyword would remove the shift (e.g., 'monkey' vs 'baby'), the joke fails as a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic Conflict = Safety + Violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is created from the overlap between safety (a trust or non-threatening frame) and violation (a break of expectation/norm). Comedic conflict is the sweet spot where both coexist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violation alone is too threatening; pure safety is boring. Effective comedy manages both — move the audience into violation while preserving enough safety (via delivery/personality, vagueness, or tone) to allow laughter rather than disgust or disengagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective violations can be: violation of a norm, word-based/linguistic (puns), violation of predictions (pattern break/three-count), and violation of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these violation types as tactical tools. Examples: puns (linguistic), the third-item break in a three-count, absurd logical conclusions, and cultural-norm breaches. Choose a violation appropriate to your comedic space and audience safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety: Create a Safe Space Through Delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Even edgy material needs a safe delivery frame so the audience feels allowed to laugh; safety can be built via likability, lightheartedness, calmness, or deliberate vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians like Lewis Black, Sarah Silverman, Anthony Jeselnik, and Amy Schumer create safety differently (tone, persona, vagueness). Keep violent/edgy specifics minimal if they threaten audience safety. Too much violation without safety leads to nervous laughs or audience disengagement (checking phones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape Comedic Space Early
rubrics_metrics.description: A top priority onstage is to shape your comedic space: establish trust (safety) while also indicating there will be violations to explore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may involve getting an early laugh or otherwise setting tone/persona so the audience 'trusts' you. Without shaping the space, subsequent violation may be rejected. Examples: Stephen Wright's early tone, Eddie Izzard's manipulation of belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-View (POV) as Source of Comedic Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Your POV is the main way of creating comedic tension — losing POV loses comedic conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid starting writing sessions by brainstorming random topics (the guide calls brainstorming destructive to creativity). Authentic, personal POV yields natural comedic conflict; manufactured topics often sound forced and inauthentic.
